"Crooked" has two distinct meanings — one physical, one moral — and both are important and widely used. Let's cover each one completely.
Meaning 1: Not straight; bent, twisted, or uneven

"Crooked" describes anything that deviates from being straight, flat, level, or properly aligned. If something should be straight but isn't — if it bends, curves, leans, or sits at the wrong angle — it is crooked.

Think of a nail hammered badly into wood. Instead of going straight in, it bends to one side. That nail is crooked. Think of an old mountain road that constantly curves left and right instead of going straight. That road is crooked. Think of a picture frame hanging on a wall but tilted slightly to one side. That picture is hanging crooked.

The word covers a wide range of "not-straightness" — a single bend, a twist, a curve, a lean, an angle that's off. It doesn't matter whether something is a little off or a lot off; both can be called crooked.

More examples:

  • Crooked teeth — teeth that grow in irregular directions instead of straight
  • A crooked nose — a nose that is bent, often from being broken at some point
  • A crooked spine — a spine that curves sideways instead of running straight down the back
  • Crooked handwriting — letters that go up and down unevenly rather than following a straight line
  • A crooked path through the forest — a path that winds and turns constantly

One nuance worth knowing: We tend to use "crooked" when something looks off or should be straight but isn't. A river naturally curves and winds, and in everyday speech people freely call it "a crooked river." But if an engineer designs a road with planned curves, you'd typically call those "curves" or "bends," not crookedness — though informally, "crooked road" is still very common and widely understood.

The second meaning is figurative — based on a very old and natural human idea: a straight path = honesty and goodness; going off the straight path = dishonesty and moral failure. So just as something physically "crooked" bends away from the straight line, a person who is morally "crooked" bends away from honesty and the law.

In this sense, "crooked" means fraudulent, corrupt, or criminal — acting dishonestly for personal gain, often by abusing a position of trust or power. It's a strong, accusatory word.

Examples:

  • A crooked politician takes bribes, abuses power, or manipulates the system for personal benefit instead of serving the public.
  • A crooked cop is a police officer who breaks the very laws they're supposed to enforce — perhaps accepting bribes to look the other way, or falsifying evidence.
  • A crooked deal is a business transaction built on deception, where one party is being cheated.
  • A crooked accountant falsifies financial records — perhaps to help a client evade taxes or hide stolen money.
  • A crooked scheme is a fraudulent plan designed to trick people out of money or rights.

This meaning is informal in register — very natural in everyday speech, in journalism, and in novels, but in formal legal documents or academic papers, you'd more often see words like corrupt, fraudulent, or dishonest. That said, "crooked" is completely standard, widely understood, and carries real punch when used.
How do you always know which meaning is being used?

Context makes it almost impossible to confuse the two:

  • If the sentence is about a physical object — a road, a nail, a tooth, a frame, a tree — it's the physical meaning.
  • If the sentence is about a person, an organization, a deal, or a plan — it's almost certainly the dishonesty meaning.

"The old fence was completely crooked" → physically bent and uneven.
"That real estate agent is completely crooked" → dishonest and likely criminal.

You will almost never encounter a sentence where both meanings seem equally possible. Context resolves it immediately, every time.

This phrase deserves its own mention because it's extremely common and it can surprise learners. A crooked smile (or crooked grin) is purely physical — it means one side of the mouth is raised higher than the other, making the smile lopsided or asymmetrical. It has nothing to do with dishonesty. In fact, in literature and everyday speech, a crooked smile is very often described as charming, roguish, or attractive. You'll encounter it constantly in novels and films, so it's worth remembering.

The word crook, as a noun, directly shares the dishonest meaning of "crooked." A crook is simply a dishonest person or a criminal. "Don't trust him — he's a crook." If someone calls a person crooked, they're calling them a crook.

• Crookedly (adverb): The painting hung crookedly. / He smiled crookedly at her.
  • Crookedness (noun): The crookedness of the hallway made it hard to move furniture. / The crookedness of local government officials made headlines.

Like most adjectives, "crooked" works with degree modifiers:

  • Slightly crooked — barely off-straight, or mildly dishonest
  • Very crooked / deeply crooked — severely bent, or profoundly corrupt
  • Completely crooked / thoroughly crooked — entirely dishonest, corrupt through and through
The single most important thing to remember

If you remember only one thing: "crooked" means "off the straight line" — physically bent in the case of objects, and morally bent in the case of people and their actions. That one core idea ties both meanings together beautifully and makes the word easy to feel intuitively, not just memorize.
